criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community domestic and multiple-use rural water service access across three local water schemes: gravity-fed piped household water connections in Tshakuma (South Africa), borehole-fed piped reticulations to public street taps in Ga-Moela (South Africa), and spring-fed piped domestic and livestock water supply to rural/farming households in Entlebuch, Kanton Luzern (Switzerland).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Plain reading: examines legal, institutional, regulatory, and collective governance arrangements shaping rural water commons under New Public Management and modernist policy regimes. Narrow 2026-10-13 reading: although framed theoretically around modernist/neoliberal imaginaries and collective solidarity ('rootedness'), the empirical case studies directly analyze rule-type mechanisms governing service access: (1) provider ownership and statutory regulatory structure (user collective/cooperative ownership vs. municipal monopoly and public-tendering requirements under South Africa's Water Services Act 1997 and Municipal Systems Act 2000 rendering CBO providers technically illegal; statutory household responsibility outside municipal built-up zones under Swiss spatial planning law SR 700; ambiguous municipal vs. community O&M mandates and upward accountability of ward-councillor-appointed unpaid borehole operators in Ga-Moela); (2) municipal discretion/accommodation (pragmatic local toleration of Tshakuma's unrecognised collective operating in a 'legal grey zone'); (3) upfront cost-recovery and membership eligibility rules (mandatory equal cash and labour contributions to join and a post-construction membership cap at 113 households in Tshakuma); and (4) public subsidy conditionalities and water-quality regulations (cantonal 60% refurbishment subsidies in Luzern conditioned on merging independent cooperatives).
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative comparative case study and action research drawing on multi-year fieldwork in South Africa (2017-2018 and 2023 follow-up, including 46 days of village residence, 6 community meetings, and 7 planning meetings in Ga-Moela) and Switzerland (2021-2023), archive/document review, and 128 semi-structured interviews (28 department officials, 12 scheme officials, 9 engineering consultants, 12 politicians, 3 academics, and 64 water users), supplemented by baseline household wealth surveys. Qualitative socio-legal/political-ecology studies are eligible for the systematic review without quantitative effect estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative water access, reliability/continuity, and exclusion outcomes: reliable piped water supply and swift breakdown repair for 113 member households in Tshakuma versus exclusion of non-contributing/late households who rely on a weaker scheme with erratic, inferior service; street-tap access in previously unserved sections of Ga-Moela alongside recurring pipe leaks, delayed municipal repair materials, elite capture (upstream tap placement for the chief allowing abstraction when other taps run dry), and shortened lines excluding tail-end households; and ongoing domestic/farm water supply reliability and breakdown pressures among 14 rural households in Entlebuch.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (rural water schemes/collectives and constituent households in Tshakuma [113 member households in a >4,000-household village], Ga-Moela [two village sections in a ~100-household village], and Entlebuch [14 farming/rural households in a cooperative], with N=128 interviewees), exposure (collective/cooperative ownership, statutory municipal monopoly/tendering rules, municipal-volunteer co-management, upfront contribution/membership cap rules, and subsidy/regulatory conditionalities), outcome (household/tap connection, continuity/breakdown maintenance, and exclusion/inferior service), and study design (qualitative multi-site comparative case study with action research) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: We base our analysis on research findings in three case studies of local water commons. The first case study describes user-initiated and constructed schemes situated in Tshakuma, a rural-peri-urban village in Vhembe district in Limpopo province, South Africa. Users own, manage, and maintain these water schemes independently from public institutions.

Especially the Water Service Act (WSA) of 1997 and the Municipal Systems Act (MSA) of 2000 had a transformational effect on the role foreseen for communities in water service provision. Community-based initiatives from then on would have to be recognized as water service providers by local government. This was only possible if no government institution could provide these services, and they would have to follow a process of public tendering designed for private service deliverers.

Households outside the built-up zone of the Kanton of Luzern are responsible for establishing and maintaining their water access [99]. This traditionally affects farming households and has led to various collectively organised water schemes especially in the mountainous regions of the Kanton. These collectives are usually organized as cooperatives and own and operate water infrastructure collectively.

In this article, we apply the Rooted Water Collectives (RWC) framework to describe two such schemes, one in South Africa and one in Switzerland. The data collection followed an action research methodology, with the main author being involved in interventions in all three schemes.

This allows him to abstract water also when the taps of others run dry. Another example is the shortening of the lines to tail-end households, due to budget constraints.

raw_response.exposure: User collective/cooperative water scheme ownership and governance interacting with statutory service-provider regulation (South Africa WSA 1997 and MSA 2000 tendering rules rendering CBOs technically illegal and reliant on municipal toleration; Swiss spatial planning self-supply mandate SR 700), upfront cash/labour membership eligibility and capacity cap rules, ambiguous municipal-community co-management with unpaid ward-appointed operators, and public capital subsidy merger/modernization conditionalities.
raw_response.outcome: Household piped water connection and street-tap access, service continuity and swiftness of breakdown repair, and household exclusion or relegation to erratic/inferior supply (including exclusion of non-contributing or post-cap households in Tshakuma and upstream elite tap capture and shortened tail-end lines in Ga-Moela).
raw_response.population_and_sample: Three rural water collectives and their user households in Limpopo Province, South Africa (Muhovhoya section of Tshakuma serving 113 households within a >4,000-household village; two sections of Ga-Moela in a ~100-household village) and Kanton Luzern, Switzerland (Entlebuch cooperative serving 14 rural/farming households); primary qualitative sample of 128 semi-structured interviewees (64 water users, 28 department officials, 12 scheme officials, 9 engineering consultants, 12 politicians, and 3 academics).
raw_response.rationale: Full-text empirical qualitative comparative case study and action research paper examining household and community domestic/multiple-use rural water supply across three user-managed schemes in South Africa and Switzerland. Satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain reading and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because it empirically analyzes provider ownership and statutory regulatory structures (cooperative/user ownership vs. municipal water service monopoly and tendering rules under South Africa's WSA 1997/MSA 2000 and Swiss spatial planning law), municipal discretion toward 'legal grey zone' CBO schemes, upfront contribution and membership-cap eligibility rules, municipal-volunteer accountability structures, and subsidy merger conditionalities, linking them directly to household connection, reliability/continuity, and exclusion outcomes. Qualitative socio-legal studies are included for mechanism synthesis even without quantitative effect estimates.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative multi-site comparative case study and action research (semi-structured interviews, participant observation/action research, and archive/document review)
